title: Dependency Injection & App Structure
scopeHtml: Scope: DI options in Swift, constructor injection, environment-based injection, containers, Hilt comparison, app entry point, scenes.

notes.title: Baseline and why DI looks different on iOS
notes.html:
Baseline for this track. Swift 6 language mode, Xcode 16+, iOS 17/18 as the minimum target, SwiftUI-first with UIKit essentials. We use @Observable, the SwiftUI App lifecycle, async/await, actors and Swift Testing. Legacy forms (AppDelegate-only apps, singletons, XCTest) are labelled "old codebases". Anything new in iOS 18/26 is marked verify.

Android equivalent first. In Android you use Hilt (Dagger) or Koin. Hilt generates code at compile time, creates components scoped to Application, Activity, ViewModel and so on, and injects with @Inject and @HiltViewModel. In iOS there is no standard DI framework and no component scoping tied to lifecycles. Most apps use plain constructor injection with a hand-written composition root, and add a library only when the wiring becomes painful.

Android iOS
Hilt @Inject constructor Plain init(dependencies...)
@Module + @Provides Factory functions / a Dependencies struct
@Singleton One instance created at the composition root (not a global static let shared)
@ViewModelScoped, @ActivityScoped Instance owned by the view via @State, or by a parent
@HiltAndroidTest + @TestInstallIn Pass fakes in the initialiser; override in test
Koin module { single {} } Factory, Swinject, swift-dependencies
Application.onCreate @main App init() / AppDelegate
Activity Scene / WindowGroup

Why it is different. Swift has no runtime reflection suitable for DI, no annotation processing like kapt/KSP in the language, and structs/protocols make manual injection cheap. The compiler already tells you if a dependency is missing, because the initialiser would not compile. Frameworks therefore add convenience, not necessity.

Real industry examples. Many successful apps (including large ones) use hand-written containers: a struct AppDependencies created in @main. Uber built Needle (compile-time DI for Swift); Airbnb uses internal tooling; Point-Free popularised swift-dependencies; Factory (by Michael Long) is a popular lightweight container.

Analogy. Android DI frameworks are a restaurant kitchen with a head chef who assembles dishes. iOS DI is usually you cooking at home: you hand the ingredients to the recipe yourself.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "iOS has no DI". It has patterns and libraries; it just has no official one.
  • Expecting lifecycle scopes. There is no Activity or ViewModel scope in SwiftUI.
  • Treating a static let shared as DI. That is a service locator or global state.

notes.title: Constructor injection and protocols
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Kotlin you write class Repo @Inject constructor(api: Api) and Hilt supplies api. Without a framework, you pass it yourself. iOS does exactly the same, and the idiomatic way is initialiser injection with a protocol type.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
protocol ProductAPI: Sendable {
    func search(_ query: String) async throws -> [ProductDTO]
}

struct LiveProductAPI: ProductAPI {
    let session: URLSession
    let baseURL: URL

    func search(_ query: String) async throws -> [ProductDTO] {
        var comps = URLComponents(url: baseURL.appending(path: "search"), resolvingAgainstBaseURL: false)!
        comps.queryItems = [URLQueryItem(name: "q", value: query)]
        let (data, response) = try await session.data(from: comps.url!)
        guard (response as? HTTPURLResponse)?.statusCode == 200 else { throw APIError.badStatus }
        return try JSONDecoder().decode([ProductDTO].self, from: data)
    }
}

struct DefaultProductRepository: ProductRepository {
    private let api: any ProductAPI          // depends on the abstraction
    init(api: any ProductAPI) { self.api = api }
}
interface ProductApi { suspend fun search(query: String): List<ProductDto> }

class DefaultProductRepository @Inject constructor(
    private val api: ProductApi
) : ProductRepository

@Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
abstract class ApiModule {
    @Binds abstract fun bindApi(impl: RetrofitProductApi): ProductApi
}

Why protocols help. A test passes a FakeProductAPI that returns canned data; no network, no mocking framework needed. Swift protocols with async requirements make fakes tiny:

struct FakeProductAPI: ProductAPI {
    var result: Result<[ProductDTO], Error>
    func search(_ query: String) async throws -> [ProductDTO] { try result.get() }
}

any vs some vs generics.

  • any ProductAPI (existential): flexible, can be swapped at runtime, small dynamic dispatch cost and a heap-allocated box for large conforming values. Swift 6 mode requires the explicit any keyword. It is fine for dependencies.
  • Generic parameter Repo<API: ProductAPI>: static dispatch and specialisation, but the generic leaks through every type that holds it. Avoid for deep graphs.
  • some ProductAPI as a parameter works as sugar for a generic (iOS 16+/Swift 5.7).

Closures as dependencies. For single-function dependencies, a struct of closures is lighter than a protocol and is the style used by Point-Free:

struct FactClient: Sendable {
    var fetch: @Sendable (Int) async throws -> String
}
extension FactClient {
    static let live = FactClient { n in /* URLSession call */ "..." }
    static let mock = FactClient { _ in "test fact" }
}

Defaults in initialisers. A tempting shortcut is init(api: ProductAPI = LiveProductAPI.shared). It reads well but hides the real dependency graph in default arguments and drags production code into previews. Use it sparingly, and never for things that talk to network or disk.

Sendable and actors. In Swift 6, anything passed into a Task or stored in a Sendable type must itself be Sendable. Make dependencies Sendable structs, or actors if they hold mutable state. A non-Sendable class dependency used from a @MainActor view model compiles; used across tasks, it produces strict concurrency errors.

Real examples. Apple's own samples inject URLSession and model containers. Apps like Signal-iOS and Wikipedia-iOS use protocol-based injection with composition roots built by hand.

Analogy. Sockets on a power strip: the lamp only needs a standard plug and does not care whether the electricity comes from the grid or a generator.

Common interview traps.

  • Injecting concrete classes and then being unable to test.
  • Protocol with associatedtype used as a stored property without any, giving the "can only be used as a generic constraint" error.
  • Forgetting Sendable in Swift 6 and hitting data race diagnostics.
  • Over-abstracting: a protocol with one implementation and no test seam is noise.

notes.title: The composition root and manual containers
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Hilt the @HiltAndroidApp Application class and generated components are the composition root. Without a framework, iOS uses the @main App struct (or AppDelegate) as the single place where concrete types are created.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct AppDependencies: Sendable {
    let productRepository: any ProductRepository
    let authService: any AuthService
    let analytics: any AnalyticsClient

    static func live(config: AppConfig) -> AppDependencies {
        let session = URLSession(configuration: .default)
        let api = LiveProductAPI(session: session, baseURL: config.apiBaseURL)
        return AppDependencies(
            productRepository: DefaultProductRepository(api: api),
            authService: KeychainAuthService(),
            analytics: LiveAnalytics()
        )
    }

    static let preview = AppDependencies(
        productRepository: FakeProductRepository(),
        authService: FakeAuthService(),
        analytics: NoopAnalytics()
    )
}

@main
struct MyApp: App {
    private let dependencies = AppDependencies.live(config: .current)

    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            RootView(dependencies: dependencies)
        }
    }
}
@HiltAndroidApp
class MyApp : Application()

@Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
object AppModule {
    @Provides @Singleton fun api(client: OkHttpClient, config: AppConfig): ProductApi =
        Retrofit.Builder().baseUrl(config.baseUrl).client(client).build().create()

    @Provides @Singleton fun repo(api: ProductApi): ProductRepository = DefaultProductRepository(api)
}

Factories for feature wiring. A feature needs a view model built from the app's dependencies. Create it in a factory or builder rather than inside the view:

@MainActor
struct FeatureFactory {
    let deps: AppDependencies

    func makeProductList() -> some View {
        ProductListView(viewModel: ProductListViewModel(repository: deps.productRepository))
    }
    func makeCheckout() -> some View {
        CheckoutView(viewModel: CheckoutViewModel(auth: deps.authService))
    }
}

A view that owns its view model gets it in init, assigned to @State:

struct ProductListView: View {
    @State private var viewModel: ProductListViewModel
    init(viewModel: @autoclosure @escaping () -> ProductListViewModel) {   // lazy: avoids building a VM per view re-init
        _viewModel = State(initialValue: viewModel())
    }
    var body: some View { Text("\(viewModel.items.count)") }
}

Note: State(initialValue:) evaluates its argument every time the parent re-creates this view struct, although SwiftUI keeps only the first result. With a heavy view model this is wasteful; keep init of view models cheap and start work in .task.

Scopes without a framework.

  • App-scoped: created once in @main, stored in let or @State.
  • Session-scoped (logged-in user): create a SessionDependencies after login and drop it at logout, which cleanly clears caches. This is the iOS answer to "user component" in Dagger.
  • Screen-scoped: a view model owned by @State.

Real examples. The open-source Wikipedia and Signal iOS apps, and many Swift sample projects, use explicit dependency structs. Airbnb's engineering posts describe dependency graphs passed through builders.

Analogy. A composition root is the stage manager who sets the props before the curtain rises; actors (features) never fetch props themselves.

Common interview traps.

  • Constructing concrete services deep inside views or view models.
  • Letting the dependency struct grow into a god object that every feature takes in full. Pass only what a feature needs.
  • Forgetting to clear session-scoped objects on logout (stale user data bug).

notes.title: SwiftUI Environment as dependency injection
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Compose the closest thing is CompositionLocal (LocalContext.current, custom LocalAnalytics). SwiftUI's Environment is that: a value propagated down the view tree, overridable on subtrees.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
// iOS 17+: @Observable objects go directly into the environment
@Observable
@MainActor
final class SessionStore {
    var user: User?
}

@main
struct MyApp: App {
    @State private var session = SessionStore()

    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            RootView().environment(session)
        }
    }
}

struct ProfileView: View {
    @Environment(SessionStore.self) private var session
    var body: some View { Text(session.user?.name ?? "Guest") }
}
val LocalSession = compositionLocalOf<SessionStore> { error("No session provided") }

@Composable
fun App() {
    val session = remember { SessionStore() }
    CompositionLocalProvider(LocalSession provides session) { RootScreen() }
}

@Composable
fun ProfileScreen() {
    val session = LocalSession.current
    Text(session.user?.name ?: "Guest")
}

Custom environment keys for protocols. For non-Observable services, define an EnvironmentKey. The modern form uses the @Entry macro (Xcode 16, back-deployable, verify):

extension EnvironmentValues {
    @Entry var analytics: any AnalyticsClient = NoopAnalytics()
}

struct CheckoutButton: View {
    @Environment(\.analytics) private var analytics
    var body: some View {
        Button("Pay") { analytics.track("pay_tapped") }
    }
}

#Preview {
    CheckoutButton().environment(\.analytics, PrintAnalytics())
}

Legacy form for older Xcode (old codebases):

private struct AnalyticsKey: EnvironmentKey {
    static let defaultValue: any AnalyticsClient = NoopAnalytics()
}
extension EnvironmentValues {
    var analytics: any AnalyticsClient {
        get { self[AnalyticsKey.self] }
        set { self[AnalyticsKey.self] = newValue }
    }
}

What belongs in the environment. Cross-cutting, read-mostly things: session, theme, analytics, router, feature flags, locale, modelContext. What does not belong: per-screen dependencies like a repository, because the environment is only readable inside views, not inside view models or services.

Environment limitations.

  • Only views read it; a view model cannot read @Environment. Pass what it needs through the initialiser.
  • A missing @Observable object in the environment is a runtime crash ("No Observable object of type X found"), not a compile error. Provide it at the root and in every #Preview.
  • @Environment cannot be read in a view's init. The value is only available when body is being evaluated, so patterns that build a view model from environment values need .task or onAppear plus optional state.
  • The environment is propagated through sheets and navigation destinations in most cases, but not across UIHostingController boundaries or into some UIKit-presented content, where you must re-inject (verify per context).
  • Changing a value in the environment invalidates readers of that key.

Real examples. Apple's frameworks use the environment for modelContext, dismiss, colorScheme, openURL. Point-Free's swift-dependencies explicitly avoids the environment for non-view code because of the limits above.

Analogy. The environment is the building's wiring: any room can plug into it, but the plumbing in the basement (services) cannot see the room's sockets.

Common interview traps.

  • Using the environment to deliver a repository to a view model.
  • Forgetting to inject into a #Preview or a sheet root with a separate hosting context.
  • Believing @EnvironmentObject is current: it is the legacy ObservableObject counterpart (old codebases); use @Environment(Type.self) with @Observable.

notes.title: DI containers: Factory, Swinject, swift-dependencies
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. Hilt is compile-time and heavyweight; Koin is a runtime service locator DSL. iOS libraries sit mostly on the Koin side of that spectrum, but with Swift's type safety.

Library Style Notes
Factory Static, type-safe container with property accessors Light, scope support (cached, singleton, shared), good with SwiftUI previews
Swinject Runtime registry (register, resolve) Older and popular; string/type keys; resolution failures happen at runtime
swift-dependencies Task-local, key-based @Dependency Comes with TCA; override per test or preview; designed for async/await
Needle (Uber) Compile-time code generation Compile-time safety like Dagger; needs a generator step (maintenance level: verify)
Resolver Older runtime container Largely superseded (verify)

Factory example (verify against the current major version).

import FactoryKit   // package product name changed in Factory 2.5: verify

extension Container {
    var productRepository: Factory<any ProductRepository> {
        self { DefaultProductRepository(api: self.productAPI()) }
            .singleton
    }
    var productAPI: Factory<any ProductAPI> {
        self { LiveProductAPI(session: .shared, baseURL: Config.apiBaseURL) }
    }
}

@MainActor
final class ProductListViewModel {
    @ObservationIgnored
    @Injected(\.productRepository) private var repository      // resolved lazily on first use
}

// In a test:
// Container.shared.productRepository.register { FakeProductRepository() }

Note on @Observable plus property wrappers: @Observable macro rewrites stored properties, so wrapper-based injected properties inside an @Observable class need @ObservationIgnored. This is a common compile error and a good interview detail.

swift-dependencies example.

import Dependencies

struct AnalyticsClient: Sendable {
    var track: @Sendable (String) -> Void
}

extension AnalyticsClient: DependencyKey {
    static let liveValue = AnalyticsClient(track: { Telemetry.send($0) })
    static let testValue = AnalyticsClient(track: { _ in })          // tests must override or fail on unexpected use
    static let previewValue = AnalyticsClient(track: { print($0) })
}

extension DependencyValues {
    var analytics: AnalyticsClient {
        get { self[AnalyticsClient.self] }
        set { self[AnalyticsClient.self] = newValue }
    }
}

@Observable @MainActor
final class CheckoutModel {
    @ObservationIgnored @Dependency(\.analytics) var analytics
    func pay() { analytics.track("pay") }
}

// Override in a test:
// let model = withDependencies { $0.analytics = .init(track: { events.append($0) }) } operation: { CheckoutModel() }

Decision guide.

  • Under about 20 services and a small team: hand-written dependency struct. Zero dependencies.
  • Want less wiring plus lazy singletons and test overrides: Factory.
  • Already using TCA or want per-test overrides propagated through async tasks: swift-dependencies.
  • Huge codebase needing compile-time graph validation: Needle or an internal generator.
  • Avoid runtime string-based resolution in new code if you can; a mis-registered type crashes only when that path executes.

Real examples. Uber (Needle), Point-Free apps (swift-dependencies), many indie and mid-size apps (Factory), and long-lived enterprise codebases (Swinject, often with Storyboards).

Analogy. A container is a vending machine: you press a button for a type and a configured object drops out, but if nobody stocked the slot, you only find out when you press it.

Common interview traps.

  • Using a runtime container as a global service locator everywhere, so dependencies become invisible.
  • Forgetting @ObservationIgnored on injected properties in an @Observable class.
  • Believing Swinject offers Hilt-style compile-time checks. It does not.
  • Registering a singleton that holds user data and never resetting it at logout.

notes.title: App, Scene, WindowGroup and @main
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Android the entry points are Application (process-wide), Activity (a screen host with a lifecycle), and the manifest. In iOS the entry point is a type marked @main conforming to App. It declares Scenes, each holding a window's content. A Scene is roughly the Activity-and-task concept: on iPhone you normally have one; on iPad and Mac the user can open several.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
import SwiftUI

@main
struct MyApp: App {
    @UIApplicationDelegateAdaptor(AppDelegate.self) private var appDelegate
    @State private var router = Router()
    @Environment(\.scenePhase) private var scenePhase

    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            RootView()
                .environment(router)
        }
        .onChange(of: scenePhase) { _, phase in
            if phase == .background { /* flush analytics, save drafts */ }
        }
    }
}
@HiltAndroidApp
class MyApp : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() { super.onCreate() /* init SDKs */ }
}

@AndroidEntryPoint
class MainActivity : ComponentActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContent { RootScreen() }
    }
}
Concept Android iOS
Process entry Application.onCreate App.init() and AppDelegate.application(_:didFinishLaunchingWithOptions:)
Screen host Activity Scene with WindowGroup (backed by UIWindowScene)
Manifest AndroidManifest.xml Info.plist + entitlements + capabilities
Multi-window Multi-window / multi-instance Multiple scenes on iPad, Mac
Background tasks WorkManager BGTaskScheduler, background modes (verify per task type)

App rules.

  • The @main attribute generates the program entry point. There must be exactly one in the app target.
  • App.init() runs once per process launch. Keep it fast: heavy work here counts toward launch time and the watchdog (around 20 seconds hard kill on launch, with much lower targets recommended; verify current numbers, aim for under 400 ms to first frame as the common guidance).
  • WindowGroup creates a window per scene. The content closure is called for each new scene. Storing shared dependencies in the App struct and passing them in keeps them shared across scenes.
  • Other scenes: DocumentGroup, Settings (macOS), Window (macOS, iOS 17+ visionOS, verify), WKNotificationScene, and ImmersiveSpace (visionOS).

AppDelegate adaptor. SwiftUI's lifecycle has no direct hooks for push-token registration, some SDK initialisations, or background URLSession events. Bridge with @UIApplicationDelegateAdaptor:

final class AppDelegate: NSObject, UIApplicationDelegate {
    func application(_ application: UIApplication,
                     didFinishLaunchingWithOptions launchOptions: [UIApplication.LaunchOptionsKey: Any]? = nil) -> Bool {
        // third-party SDK setup (Firebase, Sentry): keep it light
        return true
    }

    func application(_ application: UIApplication,
                     didRegisterForRemoteNotificationsWithDeviceToken deviceToken: Data) {
        let hex = deviceToken.map { String(format: "%02x", $0) }.joined()
        // send hex to backend
    }
}

Dependencies created in the delegate are not directly visible to the App struct. Either create the dependency container as a static or let the delegate own the container and read it in App. This is a real friction point; a common pattern is a single AppDependencies created in App.init and handed to the delegate afterwards (verify ordering in your OS version because the adaptor's delegate is created by the system).

Legacy lifecycle (old codebases). AppDelegate with UIWindow created in application(_:didFinishLaunchingWithOptions:), then from iOS 13 a SceneDelegate with scene(_:willConnectTo:options:) creating the UIWindow, root view controller and wiring UIHostingController for SwiftUI. Storyboard apps load the initial controller from Main.storyboard through the UIMainStoryboardFile Info.plist key.

Real examples. Apps like Firebase-integrated sample apps put FirebaseApp.configure() in the delegate adaptor. Sentry and Crashlytics are initialised as early as possible so launch crashes are recorded.

Analogy. The App is the theatre building, a Scene is a stage, and a WindowGroup is the rule for building another identical stage when the audience asks for one.

Common interview traps.

  • Putting network calls in App.init, which delays first frame and may trip launch watchdogs.
  • Thinking @State in App is recreated on each scene: it lives for the app struct, not per scene (use @State in the root view for per-scene state).
  • Mixing up Scene with a screen. It is a window-level container.
  • Adding two @main entries (build error "multiple @main attributes").

notes.title: Scene lifecycle and scenePhase
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Android you observe Lifecycle.Event.ON_START / ON_STOP through LifecycleEventObserver or repeatOnLifecycle. In iOS you read scenePhase from the environment, which has three values: .active, .inactive, .background.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
struct RootView: View {
    @Environment(\.scenePhase) private var scenePhase
    @State private var session = SessionStore()

    var body: some View {
        ContentView()
            .onChange(of: scenePhase) { oldPhase, newPhase in
                switch newPhase {
                case .active:     Task { await session.refreshIfStale() }
                case .inactive:   break                 // app switcher, incoming call, Control Center
                case .background: session.persistDrafts()
                @unknown default: break
                }
            }
    }
}
@Composable
fun RootScreen(session: SessionStore) {
    val owner = LocalLifecycleOwner.current
    DisposableEffect(owner) {
        val obs = LifecycleEventObserver { _, event ->
            when (event) {
                Lifecycle.Event.ON_START -> session.refreshIfStale()
                Lifecycle.Event.ON_STOP -> session.persistDrafts()
                else -> Unit
            }
        }
        owner.lifecycle.addObserver(obs)
        onDispose { owner.lifecycle.removeObserver(obs) }
    }
}

Phase meaning.

iOS phase Meaning Rough Android analogue
.active Foreground and receiving events RESUMED
.inactive Foreground but not interactive (app switcher, interruption) STARTED but not focused / onPause
.background Not visible; the system may suspend then terminate STOPPED

Important differences.

  • scenePhase read at the App/Scene level aggregates all scenes; read inside a view for that view's scene.
  • A backgrounded app is suspended within seconds, and your code stops running. Request extra time with UIApplication.beginBackgroundTask (about 30 seconds, verify), or use BGTaskScheduler, or background URLSession.
  • The system can terminate a suspended app silently without any callback (no onDestroy). Save state on .background, not at termination. applicationWillTerminate is rarely called.
  • A cold launch goes straight to .active after passing through .inactive; do not treat .active as "resumed from background" only.
  • Use .task on the root view for foreground-bound work; it is cancelled when the view disappears but a root view does not disappear on backgrounding.
  • Secure screens: show a blur or privacy view on .inactive so the app switcher snapshot does not reveal sensitive data (banking apps do this).

Legacy callbacks (old codebases). applicationDidBecomeActive, applicationWillResignActive, applicationDidEnterBackground, applicationWillEnterForeground, and the scene equivalents sceneDidBecomeActive, sceneWillResignActive, sceneDidEnterBackground, sceneWillEnterForeground. NotificationCenter observers for UIApplication.didEnterBackgroundNotification appear in Combine-era code.

Production incidents. 0x8badf00d watchdog termination (the app took too long in a lifecycle callback or held a file lock when suspended; shows up in crash logs as exception code 0x8badf00d), data loss from saving only on terminate, and websockets that silently die after suspension because the code never reconnects on .active.

Real examples. Spotify and Netflix pause playback or analytics on transitions; messaging apps reconnect sockets on .active; banking apps blur the UI on .inactive.

Analogy. Phases are like a shop: open and serving customers (active), lights on but a customer interrupts (inactive), closed and locked up with nobody checking the till (background).

Common interview traps.

  • Saving state only in applicationWillTerminate.
  • Assuming the app keeps running in .background as an Android Service would.
  • Treating .inactive as background. A phone call banner or Control Center pull-down triggers .inactive only.
  • Triggering heavy refresh on every .active, including a quick Control Center peek.

notes.title: Configuration per environment and feature flags
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Android you use buildTypes and productFlavors (debug, staging, release), BuildConfig fields, local.properties and Remote Config. In iOS the equivalents are build configurations (Debug, Release, plus custom ones like Staging), .xcconfig files, schemes, and Info.plist substitutions.

Android iOS
buildTypes { debug, release } Build configurations in the project (Debug, Release, Staging)
productFlavors Targets or schemes + xcconfig
BuildConfig.API_URL Info.plist value filled from an xcconfig variable
local.properties / secrets plugin Git-ignored Secrets.xcconfig
applicationIdSuffix Different PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER per configuration
Firebase Remote Config Firebase Remote Config / LaunchDarkly / Statsig

xcconfig example (plain text, one per configuration).

// Staging.xcconfig
PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER = com.example.myapp.staging
API_BASE_HOST = staging-api.example.com
APP_DISPLAY_NAME = MyApp (Staging)

Reference the values in Info.plist so the app can read them at runtime:

<key>APIBaseHost</key>
<string>$(API_BASE_HOST)</string>
<key>CFBundleDisplayName</key>
<string>$(APP_DISPLAY_NAME)</string>
struct AppConfig: Sendable {
    let apiBaseURL: URL
    let isDebugMenuEnabled: Bool

    static var current: AppConfig {
        let host = Bundle.main.object(forInfoDictionaryKey: "APIBaseHost") as? String ?? "api.example.com"
        #if DEBUG
        let debugMenu = true
        #else
        let debugMenu = false
        #endif
        return AppConfig(apiBaseURL: URL(string: "https://\(host)")!, isDebugMenuEnabled: debugMenu)
    }
}

An xcconfig value containing // (like a full URL) is parsed as a comment. Split scheme and host, or use a $() trick ($(SLASH) defined as /) which is a known annoyance.

Secrets. Do not commit API keys. A key shipped in the app bundle can be extracted, so treat client-side keys as public. Keep truly secret keys on a backend proxy. Store user tokens in the Keychain, not UserDefaults. Use CI secrets to generate a git-ignored xcconfig at build time.

Feature flags. A flag service is just another dependency behind a protocol:

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
protocol FeatureFlags: Sendable {
    func isEnabled(_ flag: Flag) -> Bool
}

enum Flag: String, Sendable { case newCheckout, aiSearch }

struct RemoteFeatureFlags: FeatureFlags {
    let cache: FlagCache                // loaded from LaunchDarkly / Remote Config at launch
    func isEnabled(_ flag: Flag) -> Bool { cache.bool(flag.rawValue) ?? false }
}

struct CheckoutEntry: View {
    @Environment(\.featureFlags) private var flags
    var body: some View {
        if flags.isEnabled(.newCheckout) { NewCheckoutView() } else { LegacyCheckoutView() }
    }
}
interface FeatureFlags { fun isEnabled(flag: Flag): Boolean }
enum class Flag(val key: String) { NewCheckout("newCheckout"), AiSearch("aiSearch") }

@Composable
fun CheckoutEntry(flags: FeatureFlags) {
    if (flags.isEnabled(Flag.NewCheckout)) NewCheckout() else LegacyCheckout()
}

Rules for flags.

  • Evaluate once per session or per screen entry to avoid UI flipping mid-flow.
  • Give each flag a safe default when the remote fetch fails, and cache the last fetched values on disk.
  • Remove flags after rollout; stale flags are a classic source of dead code.
  • Apple App Review requires that features visible to reviewers behave consistently; remote flags that change core behaviour after approval can violate guidelines (verify Guideline 2.3 and 4.0 wording before relying on this).

Real examples. Airbnb, Uber and Spotify use heavy experimentation platforms. LaunchDarkly, Statsig and Firebase Remote Config have iOS SDKs. Teams often add an in-app debug menu, enabled only in Debug and Staging, to override flags and switch environments.

Analogy. Environment config is choosing which road a delivery truck takes (staging or production); a feature flag is a light switch inside the building you can flip without rebuilding.

Common interview traps.

  • Using #if DEBUG to switch environments in code instead of configurations, which means the Release build never gets exercised against staging.
  • Storing secrets in the repo or in UserDefaults.
  • Believing App Transport Security lets you use http freely: non-HTTPS needs explicit exceptions and App Review justification.
  • A flag fetched asynchronously after first render, causing the UI to flicker from the old path to the new.

notes.title: Avoiding singletons and global state
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Android you know the problems of object Foo singletons and Application static references: hidden dependencies, leaks and hard tests. The same applies to Swift's static let shared, which is everywhere in Apple APIs (URLSession.shared, UserDefaults.standard, NotificationCenter.default).

// Anti-pattern: hidden dependency, untestable, shared mutable state
final class SessionManager {
    static let shared = SessionManager()
    var token: String?
}

final class ProfileViewModel {
    func load() async throws {
        var request = URLRequest(url: url)
        request.setValue(SessionManager.shared.token, forHTTPHeaderField: "Authorization")   // who else mutates this?
    }
}

Why it hurts.

  • Tests share state across runs; Swift Testing runs tests in parallel by default, so shared singletons create flaky tests.
  • Swift 6 strict concurrency: a mutable static var or a non-Sendable global is a compile error ("static property is not concurrency-safe"). A static let must be Sendable. This forces the issue.
  • Hidden coupling makes modularisation impossible because a feature package cannot import the app's singleton.
  • Lifetime bugs: user data surviving a logout.

Alternatives.

Need Instead of a singleton
Shared mutable state An actor instance injected where needed
App-wide read-mostly object @Observable in the Environment
Service for view models Constructor-injected protocol
Constants enum Constants { static let x = ... } is fine (immutable, Sendable)
Logging Inject a logger, or use os.Logger (it is a value type, so a global is acceptable) 
actor TokenStore {
    private var token: String?
    func current() -> String? { token }
    func update(_ new: String?) { token = new }
}

struct AuthenticatedClient: Sendable {
    let session: URLSession
    let tokens: TokenStore

    func send(_ request: URLRequest) async throws -> (Data, URLResponse) {
        var request = request
        if let t = await tokens.current() { request.setValue("Bearer \(t)", forHTTPHeaderField: "Authorization") }
        return try await session.data(for: request)
    }
}

When a singleton is acceptable. Truly process-wide, thread-safe, stateless-or-actor objects that Apple itself exposes: URLSession.shared for simple calls, Logger, UIApplication.shared in UIKit glue. Even then, wrap them behind your own injected type when you need to test.

Strict concurrency note. nonisolated(unsafe) silences the compiler for globals and is a smell: it hides a real data race. Prefer an actor or Mutex (the Synchronization module, iOS 18+, verify) over unsafe globals.

Migration of an old codebase. Step 1: introduce a protocol for the singleton. Step 2: let new code take it via initialiser, passing .shared at the composition root. Step 3: gradually replace call sites. Step 4: make the shared instance private. Do this incrementally; a big-bang rewrite is risky.

Real examples. Older Objective-C codebases are full of [Manager sharedInstance]. Modern guidance from WWDC and Point-Free favours explicit dependencies. Realm and Firebase expose .shared-style entry points, which is why their wrappers are common in repositories.

Analogy. A singleton is a communal kitchen drawer that everyone throws things into: handy until something goes missing and nobody knows who touched it.

Common interview traps.

  • Defending singletons as "thread-safe because of static let". Lazy initialisation is thread-safe; the state inside is not.
  • Using nonisolated(unsafe) to make warnings disappear.
  • Ignoring that UserDefaults.standard is a hidden global; wrap it for testability.
  • Forgetting to reset all shared state on logout.

notes.title: Putting it together: testing and previews with injected dependencies
notes.html:
Android equivalent first. In Android you replace Hilt modules with @TestInstallIn, and use @Preview composables with fake parameters. In iOS you pass fakes into initialisers or override environment/dependency values, and use #Preview the same way.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
@MainActor
struct ProductListScreenTests {
    @Test func showsErrorThenRetries() async {
        let repo = SequencedRepository(results: [.failure(TestError.offline), .success([.sample])])
        let vm = ProductListViewModel(repository: repo)

        await vm.load()
        #expect(vm.state == .failed("Offline"))

        await vm.load()
        #expect(vm.state == .content([.sample]))
    }
}

#Preview("Loaded") {
    ProductListView(viewModel: ProductListViewModel(repository: FakeProductRepository(result: .success([.sample]))))
        .environment(\.featureFlags, StaticFlags([.newCheckout]))
}

#Preview("Error") {
    ProductListView(viewModel: ProductListViewModel(repository: FakeProductRepository(result: .failure(TestError.offline))))
}
@Test fun showsErrorThenRetries() = runTest {
    val repo = SequencedRepository(Result.failure(IOException("Offline")), Result.success(listOf(Product.sample)))
    val vm = ProductListViewModel(repo)
    vm.load(); advanceUntilIdle()
    assertEquals(LoadState.Failed("Offline"), vm.state.value)
}

@Preview @Composable
fun LoadedPreview() { ProductListScreen(state = LoadState.Content(listOf(Product.sample))) }

Practices that pay off.

  • Keep previews cheap: no network, no Keychain. The AppDependencies.preview static from the composition root section serves every preview.
  • Use swift-dependencies or Factory test overrides only if you adopted them; otherwise pass fakes.
  • Inject clocks, UUID generators and Date providers (var now: @Sendable () -> Date) to make time-based tests deterministic.
  • Swift Testing runs tests in parallel; avoid shared mutable globals. Use @Suite(.serialized) for tests that cannot avoid shared state (verify trait name).
  • For UI flows, XCUITest (still XCTest-based) can launch the app with launchArguments such as -UITests and the composition root swaps in fake services. This is the iOS counterpart of a Hilt test module.
@main
struct MyApp: App {
    private let dependencies: AppDependencies = {
        ProcessInfo.processInfo.arguments.contains("-UITests")
            ? .uiTesting
            : .live(config: .current)
    }()
    var body: some Scene { WindowGroup { RootView(dependencies: dependencies) } }
}

Incident pattern. A preview crashes with "No Observable object of type X found" because a child view reads an environment object that the preview did not inject. Fix with a preview helper that wraps content in all standard environments.

Real examples. Teams at companies such as Airbnb and Lyft run large suites of snapshot tests with fake dependencies; Point-Free's TestStore fails a test if an unexpected dependency is used.

Analogy. A flight simulator: the cockpit (your feature) is real, but the sky and weather (network, clock) are scripted.

Common interview traps.

  • Previews that hit the real network and break offline.
  • Tests that depend on Date() or UUID() directly.
  • Forgetting that XCUITest cannot reach into app memory; it needs launch arguments or environment variables to select fakes.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• iOS has no official DI framework. Constructor injection with protocols (or structs of closures) and a hand-written composition root in the @main App is the baseline; libraries (Factory, Swinject, swift-dependencies, Needle) add convenience, and none give Hilt's lifecycle scopes.
  • Make dependencies Sendable (structs or actors) for Swift 6 strict concurrency; use any Protocol for flexibility.
  • SwiftUI Environment is the CompositionLocal analogue: great for cross-cutting values (session, router, flags, theme) and @Observable objects via @Environment(Type.self), but it is only readable by views, crashes at runtime if missing, and cannot be read in init.
  • The app starts at @main App with WindowGroup scenes; use @UIApplicationDelegateAdaptor for push tokens and SDK setup; keep launch work minimal to avoid watchdog kills.
  • scenePhase (active, inactive, background) replaces Android lifecycle observers; save state on .background, never rely on termination callbacks, and expect suspension.
  • Configure environments with build configurations and xcconfig files, never commit secrets, store tokens in the Keychain, and put feature flags behind an injected protocol with safe defaults.
  • Avoid static let shared and nonisolated(unsafe) globals: they block testing and modularisation and fight strict concurrency. Replace them with injected actors and protocols, migrating incrementally.
  • Test with Swift Testing and fakes through initialisers, drive #Preview from a preview dependency set, and swap services in UI tests via launch arguments.
